statement: A long strip of paper is folded in half, and then folded in half again, so it is 4 layers thick. Two straight cuts are made across the folded strip, neither of them on a fold. How many pieces of paper are there now?

choices.misconception: I ignored the folding and counted two cuts across a single strip, which gives 3 pieces.
I worked out what one cut does to the folded strip and forgot about the second cut.
I counted the places where the unfolded strip is cut, but there is one more piece than there are cuts.
I thought each cut makes 5 pieces, so two cuts make 5 + 5, but the two cuts share pieces between them.

hints: Unfold it in your head: where along the strip is it cut?
Each cut goes through every layer, so it cuts the unfolded strip in several places. A strip cut in some number of places falls into one more piece than that number.
Each cut goes through 4 layers, so the unfolded strip is cut in 4 places per cut.

solutions.reliable: The folded strip has 4 layers, and a straight cut across it goes through each layer once, making 4 cuts in the unfolded strip. Two cuts make 8 cut points, all at different places along the strip because neither cut is on a fold. A strip cut at 8 points falls into 8 + 1 = 9 pieces. The transferable idea: when folded paper is cut, unfold the cuts, count the cut points along the strip, and add one.
solutions.elegant: Check the rule on a smaller case you can test with real paper: one fold and one cut gives 2 cut points and 3 pieces. The same rule, pieces equal cut points plus one, gives 8 + 1 = 9 here.

whyOnTest: Folding multiplies every cut, and the unfold-then-count method avoids both forgetting layers and the off-by-one at the end.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
